newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says will go to China to fetch hijacker.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says will go to China to fetch hijacker.

text.p: A quasi-official agency in Taiwan said its agents would sail directly to rival China on Wednesday to fetch a Taiwanese hijacker who forced an airliner to fly to the mainland from the island last March.

The Straits Exchange Foundation said officials would sail from the Taiwan-controlled islet of Quemoy (Jinmen) to the nearby port of Xiamen to pick up Liu Shan-chung, completing the first hijacker repatriation between the long-time rivals.

"We are handling the handover as an individual case that is guided by the spirit of the repatriation agreement between us and the mainland," Lee Ching-ping, deputy secretary general of the foundation, told Reuters by telephone on Tuesday.

Taiwan and China, which have not had formal links since a civil war split them in 1949, reached unofficial consensus on hijacker repatriation in 1995 but failed to sign the accord because of subsequent political tensions.
The foundation, which handles dialogue with China in the absence of formal links, said the mainland side would be represented by the Red Cross.
"We will receive Liu Shan-chung from the Red Cross, sail back to Quemoy and fly back to Taiwan," Lee said.
Lee denied that the direct crossing between Quemoy and Xiamen -- separated by only a few kilometres -- violated a long-standing ban on direct travel to and from the mainland.
"This is a special case, so it cannot count as a direct link," Lee said. "We have always taken back Taiwan criminals in the mainland by this route and method."

Liu, an unemployed reporter, commandeered a Taiwan commercial jet to Xiamen on March 10, becoming the first hijacker in the 1990s to force a passenger plane from the island to the mainland rather than the other way around.
Shortly after Liu forced the jet to Xiamen, Taiwan called on Beijing to return him and offered in exchange to repatriate two mainland hijackers who had completed their prison terms.
Taiwan has conditioned their return on a resumption of semi-official contacts and the signing of the stalled repatriation pact.
Taipei is holding 16 mainlanders who hijacked a dozen planes to Taiwan in the 1990s and were convicted of air piracy.
